title: The trap from Rounders
event: 1988 WSOP Main Event — the final hand, Johnny Chan against Erik Seidel
blurb: The final hand of the 1988 World Series, made famous by the film Rounders — and by what Seidel, who went on to a great career, has said about it since.
facts: Our sources do not record the stacks, the blinds, or the size of the final all-in, so the table does not show them. The flop bets — 40,000, and the raise to 90,000 — are recorded and shown.
Heads-up, Chan had the button: he called the big blind before the flop and Seidel checked, so after the flop Seidel acts first.
ending: Chan called at once and showed J♣ 9♣ — a straight since the flop, the best possible hand. He won his second world championship in a row. Seidel finished second, and years later told PokerNews he thought he could have got away from the hand without losing his whole stack.

0.intro: You are Erik Seidel, heads-up for the 1988 world championship against the reigning champion, Johnny Chan. You hold Q♣ 7♦ in the big blind.

2.ask: Chan just called before the flop, and you checked. The flop is Q♠ 10♦ 8♦ — you have top pair, queens, with a weak kicker. You act first. Check or bet?

notes.check: What Seidel did. A modest hand on a connected board; checking keeps the pot small.
notes.bet: Charges the many draws on this board — jacks, nines and diamonds all connect with it.

2.why: Seidel checked. Q-10-8 with two diamonds is a board where many hands have a straight, two pair, or a big draw — top pair with a seven is not a hand that wants a big pot.
2.lesson: Connected boards with two of a suit are dangerous for one pair. The more ways the board can be beaten, the less your pair is worth.

4.ask: Chan bets 40,000. You still have top pair, weak kicker. Fold, call, or raise?

notes.fold: Too weak a fold for top pair against a small bet.
notes.call: Sees the turn at a small price and keeps the pot controlled.
notes.raise: What Seidel did. It finds out where he stands — but a raise is only good if worse hands call it, and on this board many hands that call are better.

4.why: Seidel raised to 90,000. Chan did not raise back: he only called — reluctantly, as CardPlayer and Paul Phua's accounts both describe it.
4.lesson: When a strong player only calls your raise on a dangerous board, think about what they could be hiding. Slow-playing the nuts looks exactly like this.

6.ask: The turn is the 2♠, a blank. You act first. Check or bet?

notes.check: What Seidel did. Keeps the pot from growing with a one-pair hand.
notes.bet: Gets value if Chan has a worse queen or a draw — but builds the pot against a range that has you beaten often.

6.why: Seidel checked, and Chan checked behind.
6.lesson: A check from a player who called your raise is not always weakness. With the best hand, giving you a free card can be the bait.

8.ask: The river is the 6♦. You act first, with top pair. Check, or move all in?

notes.check: Takes the hand to a cheap showdown. If Chan bets, you can decide then with more information.
notes.allin: What Seidel did. An all-in with one pair only makes money if Chan calls with a worse hand — and the hands that call an all-in here mostly beat a queen with a seven.
notes.bet: A smaller bet risks less than an all-in — but it is still a bet that mostly gets called by hands that beat you, and raised by the best of them.

8.why: Seidel moved all in and Chan called instantly with the straight. Seidel has since said he believes he could have got out of the hand without losing everything — the all-in risked the whole tournament with a hand that only beat a bluff.
8.lesson: Do not bet everything with a hand that only wins when they are bluffing. Ask: which worse hands call this? If the answer is almost none, check.

conflicts: Upswing Poker gives the flop as Q♣8♦10♥ and Seidel's hand as Q♣7♥ — the Q♣ twice, so its suits are not used. CardPlayer's suits have no duplicates and are used here.

One search summary had Seidel limping and Chan checking before the flop. CardPlayer states the opposite (Chan limped, Seidel checked), and Upswing's order — Seidel checking first on the flop and turn — agrees with CardPlayer, so that is used.
No source we found records the stacks, the blinds or the size of the river all-in. The table hides those numbers instead of inventing them.
